candidates.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
candidates.author: Aristotle
candidates.locator: Book I (Alpha), ch. 1, 980a21: the opening sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first sentence of the first systematic philosophy names the appetite that gets a reader out of bed: not duty, but the wish to know.
candidates.translator: W. D. Ross, 1908 (The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, Oxford)

candidates.quote: Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old.
candidates.author: Epicurus
candidates.locator: opening sentence; preserved in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X.122
candidates.whyThisMonth: A letter that opens by abolishing the excuse of being too early or too late: whatever the age, the morning is the right time to start.
candidates.translator: R. D. Hicks, 1925 (Loeb Classical Library, Diogenes Laertius vol. II)

candidates.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
candidates.author: Plotinus
candidates.whyThisMonth: A dawn image for the first light of the year: to see the sun the eye must first become sunlike, so the work of the morning is on the seer, not the view.
candidates.translator: Stephen MacKenna, 1917 (Plotinus: The Ethical Treatises, Medici Society)

candidates.quote: If it were customary to send little girls to school and teach them the same subjects as are taught to boys, they would learn just as fully and would understand the subtleties of all arts and sciences.
candidates.author: Christine de Pizan
candidates.work: The Book of the City of Ladies
candidates.locator: Part I, ch. 27 (Lady Reason answering Christine); Richards trans., Persea Books, p. 63
candidates.whyThisMonth: A woman in 1405 laying the first stone of an argument that would take five centuries to win: a beginning made in confidence that the proof would follow.
candidates.speaker: Lady Reason

candidates.quote: And I often say, when observing these trivial details: had Aristotle prepared victuals, he would have written more.
candidates.author: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
candidates.work: Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (Reply to Sister Philotea)
candidates.locator: the passage on the philosophies of the kitchen; A Woman of Genius, trans. Peden, Lime Rock Press, 1982
candidates.whyThisMonth: Philosophy begins wherever you are standing, including at the stove at six in the morning; Peden's is the wording, and the line is known in looser paraphrase, so the verifier should hold to her sentence.
candidates.translator: Margaret Sayers Peden, 1982 (A Woman of Genius: The Intellectual Autobiography of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz)

candidates.quote: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
candidates.author: Baruch Spinoza
candidates.locator: Part V, Proposition 42, Scholium: the closing sentence of the work
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last line of a book that took a lifetime, and it is an encouragement: the road you are beginning is hard because it is worth something.

candidates.quote: Enlightenment is man’s emergence from his self-incurred immaturity.
candidates.author: Immanuel Kant
candidates.work: An Answer to the Question: What is Enlightenment?
candidates.locator: opening sentence; Kant: Political Writings, ed. Reiss, Cambridge, 1970, p. 54
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous opening sentence in German philosophy is a verb of beginning: emergence, a walking out of a state you kept yourself in.
candidates.translator: H. B. Nisbet, 1970 (Kant: Political Writings, Cambridge University Press)

candidates.quote: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
candidates.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
candidates.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
candidates.locator: ch. 4 (answering Rousseau on the education of women)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The whole of self-government in one sentence, and the only power a morning resolution can actually deliver.

candidates.quote: It is perfectly true, as the philosophers say, that life must be understood backwards. But they forget the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.
candidates.author: Søren Kierkegaard
candidates.locator: entry IV A 164 (1843); The Journals of Søren Kierkegaard: A Selection, ed. and trans. Alexander Dru, Oxford, 1938
candidates.whyThisMonth: Permission to begin without the whole map, since understanding comes afterwards and living comes first; this is the Dru rendering as generally reprinted, which the verifier should confirm against the 1938 volume rather than the Hongs’ later wording.

candidates.quote: Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.
candidates.author: William James
candidates.work: Is Life Worth Living? (in The Will to Believe and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The pragmatist’s last word turns a January resolution into a mechanism: the belief you start the day with is part of what makes it true.

candidates.quote: For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.
candidates.author: Henri Bergson
candidates.locator: ch. I, The Evolution of Life; Mitchell trans., Henry Holt, 1911, p. 7
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the book is known by says that beginning again is not an exception to living but its definition.

candidates.author: Albert Camus
candidates.whyThisMonth: The rock is at the bottom again every morning and the man walks back down to it: the closing line makes the return itself the victory.

candidates.quote: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
candidates.author: Simone de Beauvoir
candidates.locator: Book Two, Part IV, ch. 1 (Childhood): the opening sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most quoted opening line of twentieth-century philosophy is about becoming, which is to say that who you are is still being written.

candidates.quote: Men, though they must die, are not born in order to die but in order to begin.
candidates.author: Hannah Arendt
candidates.locator: ch. V, section 34; University of Chicago Press, 1958, p. 246
candidates.whyThisMonth: Her whole doctrine of natality in one clause, the close of a longer sentence on the same page: every morning is evidence that beginning is what we are for.

candidates.quote: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
candidates.author: Simone Weil
candidates.locator: letter of 13 April 1942; English in Simone Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, trans. Rosenthal, Pantheon, 1976; French in Correspondance, L’Âge d’Homme, 1982, p. 18
candidates.whyThisMonth: The simplest thing a day can begin with is a decision about where to look; the verifier should confirm the page in Rosenthal, since that biography is where this English wording entered circulation.
candidates.translator: Raymond Rosenthal, 1976 (in Pétrement’s Simone Weil: A Life)

candidates.quote: Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real.
candidates.author: Iris Murdoch
candidates.locator: Chicago Review 13, no. 3 (Autumn 1959), p. 51; reprinted in Existentialists and Mystics, 1997
candidates.whyThisMonth: A definition to carry into the first hour with other people: the day’s work is the difficult one of noticing that they are real.
